cim: Can artificial intelligence help us understand the universe?

cim_eredeti: Can artificial intelligence help us understand the universe?
szoveg_eredeti:
MCAST study reveals insights into universe's evolution through data analysis and AI

Cosmologists have a puzzle. Estimates based on observations of the early universe and observations of nearby stars and galaxies give different answers to the same question of “How quickly is the universe expanding today?” This disagreement is known as the Hubble tension. It may point to something missing from our picture of the universe, or to details in the measurements that need further examination.

At MCAST’s Institute of Applied Sciences, the CosmoAI project brings together astrophysics, cosmology, and artificial intelligence (AI) to help researchers test possible explanations using large collections of observations. Cosmo­AI forms one part of a wider project, which is building ways to compare scientific ideas with the evidence gathered by telescopes and space missions.

Machine-learning tools can help explore patterns, while researchers check what those patterns mean and whether they fit what we know about the universe.

Ground-based telescopes and space missions collect more data than researchers can examine in a lifetime. Machine learning can help sift through these measurements, highlight patterns and compare possible theoretical models. Researchers then ask whether a pattern makes sense under the laws of physics and whether it appears in other observations too.

One strand of our research explores alternative ways the universe may have evolved. We found that some models can reproduce the broad history in our best current picture of the cosmos, while allowing other possibilities. These are ideas for further investigation, not an answer to the Hubble tension; the next step is to check them against what telescopes observe.

Finding a pattern is only one part of the job. A possible explanation has to be checked against real observations, and researchers need to be open about uncertainty. CosmoAI is developing tools to make these comparisons more systematic, while keeping the science understandable and the conclusions tied to evidence.

The research also helps build expertise in mathematics, computing and data analysis in Malta. By bringing together researchers with complementary skills and working with international colleagues, the project gives Maltese scientists a part in a much wider effort to understand the cosmos.

Cosmology asks questions that are both scientific and deeply human: how did the universe change, and what can the light reaching us reveal about its past? The answers take time. Our work is helping create better ways to test possible explanations and to see which ones stand up to what the universe shows us.

This work was developed along with Gabriel Farrugia, Rebecca Briffa, Konstantinos Dialektopoulos and Jackson Levi Said.

Mark Pace is a senior lecturer at MCAST’s Institute of Applied Sciences and principal investigator of CosmoAI, a Xjenza Malta-funded project applying machine learning to cosmology. His research focuses on theoretical astrophysics, modified gravity and computational approaches to understanding the universe’s evolution.

CosmoAI is funded through Xjenza Malta’s FUSION R&I Research Excellence Programme (REP-2025-028). A strand of the team’s work was presented at CosmoVerse 2026 in Bilbao.

• Stars are born in some of the coldest places in space. They form inside clouds of gas and dust, where gravity draws material together. As a clump contracts, its centre heats up, eventually creating a star.

• The most massive stars have the shortest lives. Despite having more fuel, they use it much faster. Some survive only a few million years, while small stars can shine for trillions.

• We are made of star stuff. Many of the elements in our bodies, such as carbon and oxygen, were forged inside stars. Released into space as stars aged and died, these ingredients eventually became part of our solar system, Earth and us. Much of our hydrogen is older still, originating in the early universe.

• Planets grow from the material surrounding newborn stars. In a spinning disc of gas and dust, particles collide and stick together, gradually building larger bodies that can become planets.

The Horsehead Nebula sits just south of Alnitak (Zeta Orionis), the easternmost star in Orion’s Belt in the Orion constellation. Astronomers estimate that its distinctive structure could disappear in about five million years as radiation from nearby stars is gradually eroding it. The Horsehead looks dramatically different in infrared light. Infrared wavelengths reveal glowing dust and structures hidden in visible-light photographs, helping astronomers investigate the cloud’s interior. Photo: Mark Pace

In July 1975, an American Apollo spacecraft and a Soviet Soyuz capsule met in orbit for a historic handshake. But before their crews could greet each other, engineers had to solve an unusual problem: how should the spacecraft connect?

Earlier docking systems often used a “male” probe that fitted into a “female” socket. For Apollo–Soyuz, engineers developed an “androgynous” connection: matching docking mechanisms that could each take either the active or passive role, called the Androgynous Peripheral Assembly System (APAS-75).

This offered practical flexibility, particularly for potential rescue missions, where compatible spacecraft might need to help one another. It also suited a mission intended to bring two rival superpowers together as equals.

A special docking module provided a passage between the spacecraft and acted as an airlock between their different cabin atmospheres.

When the hatches opened on July 17, the handshake became a symbol of cooperation during the Cold War, made possible by some carefully designed hardware.
